paras: The Goodlettsville manhunt of 1888 was a search near Goodlettsville, Tennessee, in late June 1888 by a posse or mob for an unnamed Black man accused of raping and knifing a young woman engaged to be married. Nashville dispatches said he would be lynched if caught, but no report of his capture appears in the coverage.

According to the Memphis Appeal, Fannie Garrett and Irvin Holder, described as "colored," were granted a marriage license on June 26; other versions said she worked for Charles Smiley, who had procured the license.

At about 2 a.m. on June 27, by the Appeal's account, a man called at the house, said Holder was dying of a hemorrhage, and walked her toward Holder's home just over the Sumner County line. After they crossed the bridge between Sumner and Davidson counties, the dispatch said, he seized and raped her, cutting her face, ear and hand with an open knife, then let her go under threat of death. She returned home and told Smiley.

The searchers were "a posse of citizens" in the Appeal, "a mob of people" in the Springfield Daily Republic, and "a mob of whites" in the Washington Critic, and all three said the man would be lynched if caught.
No report of the man's identification, arrest or lynching, or of any legal proceeding, was found.

The story ran as a single Nashville dispatch, first in the Memphis Appeal on June 28 under the headline "A Black Devil." On June 29 the Springfield Daily Republic in Ohio printed the same text as "Outraged on the Eve of Her Wedding," without the girl's name, while the Washington Critic condensed it into its "News of the Day" roundup. Both later versions called the accused "the brute," and none of the papers questioned the girl's account or the expected lynching.

The Appeal's dispatch dated June 27 placed the assault "this morning," while the Springfield paper printed the same words under a June 29 dateline and the Washington Critic put it "early yesterday morning" in its June 29 issue. As the earliest and only Tennessee report, the Appeal gives the date best supported by its own text.

reader.title: Goodlettsville manhunt of 1888
bases: All three reports describe a posse or mob hunting a Black man accused of rape who, they said, would be lynched if caught; no capture or killing was reported (A1, A2, A3).

A 'posse of citizens' or 'mob' was reported hunting the accused man with the stated expectation that he would be lynched, but no report says he was caught or killed (A1, A2, A3); this was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
The three reports share the same narrative and wording and appear to derive from one Nashville dispatch (A1, A3), with A2 a condensed version, so they are not independent confirmations.

accounts.label: Nashville dispatch (complainant's account)
accounts.gist: A man came at 2 a.m. saying Holder was dying, walked her toward Holder's house, seized and raped her after crossing the county-line bridge, cut her with an open knife, and threatened to kill her if she screamed; a posse was hunting him.

accounts.label: Wire roundup
accounts.gist: A condensed version: the man assaulted Smiley's servant girl at a 'secluded spot' and cut her; she gave the alarm, and 'A mob of whites' was searching for him.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headed the dispatch 'A Black Devil' and reported without comment that the man would 'probably be lynched'.
The Washington Critic ran a one-paragraph version in its roundup, calling the man 'the brute' who 'will be lynched if captured'.
The Springfield Daily Republic headed the dispatch 'Outraged on the Eve of Her Wedding' and also used 'the brute'.

versions.value: 'Early yesterday morning' in a June 29 paper (June 28)
'this morning' in a dispatch dated June 29

conflicts.note: A1 is the earliest and Tennessee report and its dateline fits its text; A3 prints the same wording under a later dateline, so June 27 is the better-supported date.
Different words for the same search party; only A2 states the searchers' race.

conflicts.field: where the girl was called from
conflicts.note: Consistent with her living at her employer's.

record_check.dossier: Fannie Garrett was the complainant in the alleged assault; the person the mob hunted (the target of the threatened lynching) was an unnamed Black man.

The man sought was described as a 'negro' or 'colored man'; the Appeal's '(colored)' follows both names in 'Fannie Garrett and Irvin Holder (colored)', so her race is likely but not unambiguously stated.

record_check.record: said to have assaulted Fannie Garrett, a colored girl
record_check.dossier: Accused of rape and knife wounds after luring her out with a false message; no article calls her 'a colored girl' in those words.
The assault was placed at the Sumner-Davidson county-line bridge; Davidson is plausible but the side is not stated.
'posse of citizens' in A1 but 'mob' in A2 and A3.
Threatened: the papers report a search with lynching expected if he was caught; no capture or attempt on his life was reported.

info: About 2 a.m. on June 27, 1888, per the Nashville dispatch of June 27; A3 dates the same text June 29, and A2 says 'early yesterday morning' (June 28)
Near Goodlettsville, Tennessee, at or just past the bridge dividing Sumner and Davidson counties, on the way to Holder's house just over the Sumner county line
The man sought by the posse was not named or identified; the complainant was Fannie Garrett (named only in A1), a servant girl at Charles Smiley's
Accused of luring the girl out at night with a false message that her fiance was dying, then raping her and cutting her with a knife
'A posse of citizens' (A1), 'A mob of people' (A3), 'A mob of whites' (A2)

sources.note: Special dispatch, Nashville, June 27, headed 'A Black Devil': names Fannie Garrett and Irvin Holder; alleged assault at the Sumner-Davidson bridge; posse of citizens hunting the man, who would 'probably be lynched'.
quotes: A posse of citizens are looking for the negro today. If he is caught he will probably be lynched.
